summary: This BIS Working Paper (No 1099) examines who holds sovereign debt and the implications for borrowing costs. The authors construct a dataset of sovereign debt holdings by investor type (banks, non-banks, official creditors) for 95 countries over 1991-2018. Key findings: private non-bank investors absorb disproportionately more sovereign debt supply than other investor groups (69% of increases despite holding 46% on average); non-bank investor demand is most responsive to yield; counterfactual analysis shows emerging market sovereigns face 6.7% cost increase per 10% debt increase, but 9% if non-bank investors were absent.
why_it_matters: Understanding sovereign debt investor composition is critical for governments' borrowing capacity and financial stability. The research demonstrates that non-bank private investors play a disproportionately large role in absorbing new debt issuance, and their presence significantly reduces borrowing costs for emerging market sovereigns.
macro_context: Research published during period of elevated global debt levels following COVID-19 pandemic. Dataset spans 1991-2018, covering multiple crisis episodes and the post-pandemic debt build-up period.
market_structure_context: The paper disaggregates sovereign debt holders into six investor groups: foreign vs domestic, and within each: private banks, non-bank private investors, and official creditors (central banks, international organizations). This granular decomposition reveals how different investor types respond to changes in debt supply.
